title: Panda: Pretrained forecasting for chaotic dynamics
one_liner: Train one model on thousands of diverse chaotic systems so it predicts unseen chaotic motion without retraining.
lead: Chaotic systems like weather and neurons are hypersensitive: tiny changes in one measurement explode into huge differences later. Today's solutions either train a fresh model for each system (slow) or use generic time-series models that ignore how chaos works. Panda trains on 20,000 synthetic chaotic systems discovered by breeding—not stealing—parameters from classic attractors. The result: one model that predicts unfamiliar chaotic motion zero-shot, and somehow works on high-dimensional systems it never saw.

problem.h2: Why chaos defeats ordinary time-series models
paras: Chaotic systems like fluid flows and brain activity have a brutal property: two states that start almost identical will end up completely different a few steps later. This is not randomness—the math is fully deterministic—but the system amplifies even tiny measurement errors into large mistakes. Building a model that predicts chaotic behavior is therefore intrinsically hard: you need to capture how the system moves in phase space (the space of all possible states), not just fit patterns in past data like a weather app.

Past approaches split into two camps: (1) Train a specialized model per system (slow and requires retraining for every new system you want to forecast). (2) Use a generic time-series foundation model trained on millions of historical data points—these models work on regular signals but often miss the underlying dynamical structure that makes chaos behave the way it does.

callout.html: Apply a standard transformer (a model that reads sequences left-to-right and looks for statistical patterns) to chaotic motion. It will predict the next few steps accurately, then diverge—because it learned surface patterns instead of the underlying equations driving the chaos.

steps.text: Evolutionary algorithm breeds 20,000 chaotic ODE systems from 129 seed attractors (Lorenz, double pendulum, etc.) by mutating and combining their parameters.
Break each trajectory into short windows (patches) using Fourier features and polynomial basis functions, reducing noise and encoding local structure.

steps.b: Step 3: Temporal attention mixes time direction
steps.text: Self-attention reads across the patches in time (with rotary positional encoding), letting the model see dependencies across future states.
Separate attention layers read across variables (x, y, z dimensions) at the same timestep, modeling how one variable steers the others.

steps.b: Step 5: Masked pretraining gently steers toward continuity
steps.text: Hide random patches during training and force the model to fill them in—this teaches the model that motion is continuous and prevents memorizing surface patterns.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the attention architecture
paras: Standard time-series models apply one global attention layer that looks only at the time dimension—they treat each variable independently and then hope they learn coupling implicitly. Panda adds two new attention layers: temporal attention (across patches in time) and channel attention (across variables at the same timestep). This dual view lets the model explicitly see how variables push each other in dynamical systems.
object.object: Attention layers: add channel dimension attention

hidden.h2: The Lyapunov exponent: how long predictions stay accurate
hidden.name: Lyapunov time (chaos strength)
paras: In chaotic systems, errors grow exponentially—each step magnifies the tiny seed error by the same factor. The Lyapunov exponent measures this magnification factor: a larger exponent means errors double faster because the system's equations push small differences apart (like stretching a rubber sheet in one direction). For forecasting, the practical question is how many steps ahead can you predict before errors blow up? The Lyapunov time is the number of timesteps it takes for an error to grow by a factor of e (about 2.7)—a natural unit because exponential growth is defined that way. Panda measures this by evolving the true system and the model-predicted system in parallel, tracking when they diverge.

The paper estimates Lyapunov exponents from the actual data using the Rosenstein method (numerical approximation from observed trajectories), then reports prediction accuracy in terms of how many Lyapunov times ahead the model stays right. This matters because different systems have vastly different chaos rates: one system might have a Lyapunov time of 5 steps, another 100 steps. Measuring accuracy in Lyapunov times (not arbitrary timesteps) makes the comparison fair and ties the results to the dynamical theory—the fundamental explanation for why chaos behaves the way it does.

heat.caption: Darker cells show stronger exponential error growth (high Lyapunov exponent). Predictions stay accurate longer when chaos is weaker.

reads.html: The Lyapunov time is how many steps until prediction error grows big from tiny seed error.

The maximum Lyapunov exponent is estimated per system trajectory using the Rosenstein estimator, then prediction accuracy is reported as steps divided by Lyapunov time, quantifying how many time-scales the model stays correct.

mechanism.h2: Why channel attention beats the alternative
paras: Standard time-series models use only temporal attention: each variable is read independently across time, then later layers combine them. This forces the model to learn inter-variable coupling implicitly from how the loss changes. In chaotic systems, variables are tightly coupled—velocity depends on position, position depends on forces, and all three change together. Univariate-only attention ignores this and makes the model solve the coupling problem the hard way.

Panda adds channel attention: at each timestep, the model sees x, y, and z together and learns their instantaneous relationships. This mirrors how physical dynamical systems actually work: forces (derivatives) depend on the current state across all dimensions. The paper shows that channel attention alone reduces error by 30 percent on multivariate systems. Combined with masked pretraining (which forces continuity), the model learns to extrapolate chaotic motion—not by memorizing time-series patterns, but by learning how coupled state variables drive each other forward.

The result is transfer: after training on 20k diverse ODE systems, the model can predict a new ODE it has never seen. Even more: it somehow predicts high-dimensional PDEs (where 10+ variables couple) despite training only on 3D systems. The theory explains why: the model learned the grammar of chaos—how variables couple, how perturbations grow, how attractors organize—not the parameters of any specific system.

stages.s: Time-series trajectory: x(t), y(t), z(t) for a chaotic ODE
Embed into Fourier + polynomial patches (16-step windows)
Temporal attention: read across patches in time with rotary encoding
Channel attention: read x, y, z variables together, not separately
Masked pretraining: hide random patches, predict them back
Forecast next 128 timesteps, preserving chaos statistics

math.words: For each batch of trajectories, randomly mask (hide) some patches. Train the model to predict the hidden patches. The loss is the mean squared error between predicted patches and true patches, summed over all masked positions.
symbols: the model-predicted trajectory for masked patch j
the ground-truth trajectory for patch j

items.b: Dimension mismatch on very high-dimensional systems.
items.html: Panda trains on 3D ODEs but zeros-shots on 10D+ PDEs. On even higher dimensions (50+), the channel attention may overfit to spurious correlations not seen during training.

The architecture assumes deterministic chaos. If the true system includes random noise (unpredictable variation) or is non-chaotic, the model's learned continuity may give false confidence in predictions.

items.b: Lyapunov times that are too short.
items.html: If the system is extremely chaotic (very large Lyapunov exponent), even one step carries significant error growth. The model cannot overcome physics.

items.b: Done right: test on systems never seen before.
items.html: Evaluate on held-out chaotic systems from the same evolutionary algorithm, then on real chaotic PDEs (like Navier-Stokes) with full cross-validation, to measure transfer honestly.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple ODE (e.g. a 3D system not in the 20k training set, created by randomly mutating Lorenz parameters). Initialize the system at a random state. Run Panda to forecast 200 steps ahead. Compare against the true system evolved with a numerical integrator. Plot both trajectories in 3D phase space and compute prediction error over time. The demo should show: short-term predictions track the true attractor shape (both stay on the butterfly wings), but diverge after 2-3 Lyapunov times as expected. Then retrain Panda without channel attention (temporal only) and show divergence happens faster, because temporal attention alone cannot see that x and y push each other—it treats them separately and misses the coupling that makes the attractor stable.
demo.metric_eq: Prediction error = sqrt(mean((forecast_state - true_state)^2)) over all timesteps, reported per Lyapunov time
demo.closing: The demo must make impossible to miss: channel attention keeps the model on the right attractor longer than temporal-only, and the model works zero-shot on systems it has never learned.
